title: The 4-Step Script Framework That Fixes Client Video Performance

slides.heading: Your Client's Script Is Losing Them Viewers
slides.subtitle: Your edit is performing fine. The script is the problem. Here is the 4-step Relatable Authority before Action framework to fix it.
slides.takeaway: The edit is the last 20% of the job. The script is the first 80%.
slides.visual: A video script document on a dark desk with visible red markup annotations and crossed-out lines, indicating a problematic script structure that needs to be rebuilt. Deep dark purple background, cinematic mood, purple accent light, high contrast, match the brand guide style.

slides.heading: Step 1: Find the Generic Hook
slides.subtitle: Read the first 3 lines out loud. Does it open with what the product does? A benefit claim? Does it assume the viewer already cares?
slides.takeaway: If yes to any of these, the hook needs rebuilding. A viewer who doesn't trust the brand scrolls past every one of those openers.
slides.visual: A script document on a dark screen with the first three lines highlighted in red, showing generic hook language being identified and flagged for revision. Deep dark purple background, cinematic mood, purple accent light, high contrast, match the brand guide style.

slides.heading: Step 2: Replace With a Pattern Interrupt
slides.subtitle: Challenge a belief the audience already holds. 85% of people dealing with acne have been treating it in the wrong order. That stops the scroll.
slides.takeaway: Don't open with the product. Open with the audience's wrong assumption.
slides.visual: A script rewrite in progress on a dark screen, the generic opening crossed out in red and a bold pattern interrupt hook written below it in white, the new line glowing with purple highlight showing the improvement. Deep dark purple background, cinematic mood, purple accent light, high contrast, match the brand guide style.

slides.heading: Step 3: Add the Credibility Layer
slides.subtitle: After the interrupt, earn the right to keep talking. One real stat or a specific piece of research. One sentence, one number, one fact.
slides.takeaway: This is what makes the viewer feel understood rather than sold to.
slides.visual: A script section on a dark screen with a single data point highlighted inside a rounded callout box, showing how one specific number or stat integrates into the script flow and builds instant authority. Deep dark purple background, cinematic mood, purple accent light, high contrast, match the brand guide style.

slides.heading: Step 4: Use Ingredient Language
slides.subtitle: Describe how it works, not what it does. Not 'Our formula clears acne.' Instead: 'This combines niacinamide and zinc to block the enzyme that triggers oil overproduction.'
slides.takeaway: Generic benefits feel like ads. Specific mechanisms feel like education.
slides.visual: Two side-by-side script lines on a dark screen, the left labeled Benefit Language showing vague product copy and the right labeled Ingredient Language showing specific mechanism-driven copy, the contrast between them stark and clear. Deep dark purple background, cinematic mood, purple accent light, high contrast, match the brand guide style.

slides.heading: Learn the Script. Keep the Client.
slides.subtitle: Editors who understand script structure don't just deliver good edits. They get kept around a lot longer.
slides.takeaway: Follow Ananda Paramanick for more on what separates editors who get consistent clients from the ones who don't.
